children.title: Reparameterization Limits
children.top_down_role: Regimes where coordinate transformations cannot economically restore favorable geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Reparameterization Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates geometric improvement under reparameterization from preservation of cheap coordinate updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the quadratic \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx-c^{\mathsf T}x\) with \(Q\succ0\), an invertible change \(x=Ty\) produces Hessian \(T^{\mathsf T}QT\). If \(T=D\) is diagonal, then for every \(i\neq j\), \[\frac{|(D^{\mathsf T}QD)_{ij}|}{\sqrt{(D^{\mathsf T}QD)_{ii}(D^{\mathsf T}QD)_{jj}}}=\frac{|Q_{ij}|}{\sqrt{Q_{ii}Q_{jj}}}.\] Hence diagonal rescaling cannot remove normalized cross-coordinate coupling. A general dense \(T\) can diagonalize or whiten \(Q\), but changing one coordinate of \(y\) moves \(x\) along a generally dense column of \(T\). Thus reparameterization cannot simultaneously guarantee decoupled curvature and preservation of sparse, constant-support updates without additional structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagonal scaling cannot remove normalized coordinate coupling; dense transformations can whiten curvature but generally turn coordinate steps into dense updates.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is symmetric positive definite.
\(T\) is invertible; diagonal entries of \(D\) are nonzero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Diagonal scaling preserves normalized coupling, while dense whitening generally destroys coordinate-update sparsity.

children.title: Global Certificate Aggregation Cost

knowledge_statements.title: Global Certificate Aggregation Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower bound for certifying full-gradient stationarity from coordinate derivative queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an oracle that, at a fixed \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), reveals one requested component \(g_i=(\nabla f(x))_i\) per unit query. Without a maintained exact aggregate or structural relation among components, any deterministic procedure certifying \(\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_\infty\le\varepsilon\) for every admissible differentiable objective must query all \(d\) components in the worst case. Indeed, after fewer than \(d\) queries, an unqueried component is compatible both with magnitude at most \(\varepsilon\) and with magnitude greater than \(\varepsilon\). Therefore one exact global stationarity check costs at least \(d\) component queries, and checks performed every \(m\) coordinate updates add amortized cost at least \(d/m\) queries per update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without cached global information or structural coupling, an exact infinity-norm stationarity check needs every gradient component, costing d queries per check.
assumptions_latex: Each oracle call returns only one exact gradient component.
Unqueried components have no known structural dependence on queried components.
The certificate must be valid for every admissible objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The worst-case certification cost is at least \(d\) component queries, or \(d/m\) amortized queries when checked every \(m\) updates.

number of coordinate updates between global checks

children.title: Full-Gradient Crossover Regimes
children.top_down_role: Problem regimes where full-gradient updates become preferable to coordinate updates.

knowledge_statements.title: Full-Gradient Crossover Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Work-based crossover condition between coordinate and full-gradient methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an accuracy criterion \(E(x)\le\varepsilon\). Let \(N_C(\varepsilon)\) and \(N_F(\varepsilon)\) be valid upper bounds on the numbers of coordinate and full-gradient updates required to meet it, and let \(c_C\) and \(c_F\) be their respective per-update costs in one common resource unit. Under an additive deterministic cost model, the full-gradient method has no larger certified total work precisely when \[c_FN_F(\varepsilon)\le c_CN_C(\varepsilon).\] If one full gradient costs \(c_F=d c_C\), the crossover condition becomes \(N_C(\varepsilon)/N_F(\varepsilon)\ge d\). Thus cheap coordinate updates cease to confer a work advantage when their required update count grows by at least the per-update cost ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full-gradient optimization crosses over when its higher per-step cost is offset by a proportionally smaller number of steps to the target accuracy.
assumptions_latex: Both iteration bounds guarantee the same error criterion and tolerance.
Per-update costs are expressed in the same additive resource unit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Full-gradient work is preferable exactly when \(c_FN_F(\varepsilon)\le c_CN_C(\varepsilon)\).

notation.meaning: cost per coordinate and full-gradient update

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projected-Gradient Energy Crossover for a Richer Subspace
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local geometric crossover under a common Euclidean smoothness model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^d	o\mathbb R\) have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, let \(S\) be a linear subspace, and let \(P_S\) be its orthogonal projector. The step \(x_S^+=x-L^{-1}P_S
abla f(x)\) satisfies \[f(x)-f(x_S^+)\ge  rac{\|P_S
abla f(x)\|^2}{2L}.\] If this update costs \(c_S>0\), while the analogous step in coordinate direction \(e_i\) costs \(c_i>0\), then the certified decrease per unit cost of \(S\) exceeds that of coordinate \(i\) whenever \[ rac{\|P_S
abla f(x)\|^2}{c_S}> rac{|
abla_i f(x)|^2}{c_i}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A richer subspace crosses over locally when its additional captured gradient energy more than offsets its additional update cost.
assumptions_latex: \nabla f\text{ is }L\text{-Lipschitz in the Euclidean norm}.
S\text{ is a linear subspace and }P_S\text{ is its orthogonal projector}.

assumptions_latex: All block sizes use the same error criterion and tolerance.
The cost model is additive and includes forming and applying each subspace update.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An optimal block size minimizes \(c_bN_b(\varepsilon)\), and size \(b\) beats scalar coordinates iff \(c_bN_b(\varepsilon)<c_1N_1(\varepsilon)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The condition is the direct comparison of certified total work under a common additive cost model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Crossover condition for replacing scalar coordinates by larger update subspaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each admissible block size \(b\in\{1,\ldots,d\}\), suppose a method updates a \(b\)-dimensional subspace, incurs cost \(c_b>0\) per update, and requires at most \(N_b(\varepsilon)\) updates to obtain \(E(x)\le\varepsilon\). Relative to scalar coordinates, size \(b\) is a certified work improvement exactly when \[c_bN_b(\varepsilon)<c_1N_1(\varepsilon),\] equivalently \(N_1(\varepsilon)/N_b(\varepsilon)>c_b/c_1\). More generally, the work-optimal supported subspace size belongs to \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{1\le b\le d}c_bN_b(\varepsilon)\). Hence a richer subspace crosses over only when its reduction in required updates exceeds its multiplicative increase in update cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A larger block is worthwhile when its reduction in update count exceeds its per-update cost increase; optimal block size minimizes total certified work.

children.title: Hardware-Driven Crossover
children.top_down_role: Computing architectures whose parallelism or memory behavior favors more informative updates.

knowledge_statements.title: Hardware-Driven Crossover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Wall-clock crossover after accounting for parallelism, latency, and bandwidth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a coordinate update perform work \(w_C\), transfer \(q_C\) bytes, expose parallelism \(p_C\), and incur latency \(\ell_C\); define analogous quantities for a richer update \(R\). On hardware with compute rate \(P\), bandwidth \(B\), and usable concurrency capped by \(p\), model update time by \[t_M=\ell_M+\max\!\left\{\frac{w_M}{P\min\{p_M,p\}},\frac{q_M}{B}\right\},\qquad M\in\{C,R\}.\] If \(N_M(\varepsilon)\) updates certify the common tolerance, the richer method crosses over in wall-clock time when \(N_R(\varepsilon)t_R<N_C(\varepsilon)t_C\). Consequently, low coordinate arithmetic cost does not imply lower runtime when coordinate work exposes little parallelism or is dominated by latency and memory traffic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hardware favors richer updates when their parallelism and data movement yield lower total wall time, even if each update performs more arithmetic.
assumptions_latex: Both methods target the same accuracy criterion.
The roofline-style time model adequately represents execution.
Update times and counts compose additively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The richer method is faster when \(N_R(\varepsilon)t_R<N_C(\varepsilon)t_C\).

notation.meaning: modeled wall time per update of method M
compute rate, memory bandwidth, and concurrency cap
updates required for the common tolerance

children.title: Information-Cost Crossover
children.top_down_role: Operating points where additional directional information outweighs its acquisition cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Information-Cost Crossover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Crossover based on certified progress per unit cost of acquired derivative information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two randomized update mechanisms \(A\) and \(B\) at state \(x\). Let \(I_M(x)>0\) be the expected cost of acquiring the derivative information used by mechanism \(M\), and let \(\Delta_M(x)=\mathbb E[f(x)-f(x_M^+)\mid x]\ge0\) be its expected one-step decrease. Under a locally stationary additive model, mechanism \(B\) has better information efficiency than \(A\) exactly when \[\frac{\Delta_B(x)}{I_B(x)}>\frac{\Delta_A(x)}{I_A(x)}.\] Equivalently, its relative progress gain exceeds its relative information cost: \(\Delta_B(x)/\Delta_A(x)>I_B(x)/I_A(x)\), when both denominators are positive. This condition marks the crossover from cheap partial information to more informative updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A richer update is preferable per information cost when its relative expected progress gain exceeds its relative cost of acquiring derivative information.
assumptions_latex: Both mechanisms are compared at the same state and objective.
Information costs are positive and measured in a common unit.
Expected one-step decreases are finite.

notation.meaning: expected derivative-information cost of mechanism M
expected objective decrease from mechanism M
the random next iterate produced by mechanism M

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Step Information Efficiency Does Not Imply Total-Run Superiority
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the seed's locally stationary efficiency comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let mechanisms \(A\) and \(B\) have state-dependent expected decreases \(\Delta_M(x)\) and information costs \(I_M(x)>0\). The inequality \[\frac{\Delta_B(x_0)}{I_B(x_0)}>\frac{\Delta_A(x_0)}{I_A(x_0)}\] at one state \(x_0\) does not by itself imply that \(B\) reaches a prescribed tolerance with smaller expected total information cost. That conclusion requires trajectory-wide comparisons or uniform progress bounds that can be accumulated into total-cost guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Better progress per information cost at one state need not imply lower information cost to convergence.
assumptions_latex: The mechanisms may generate different later states and state-dependent efficiencies.

notation.meaning: total derivative-information cost incurred before mechanism M reaches tolerance epsilon
